clue.text: Surprisingly classical English no less strangely poetic somehow

indicators.note: 'no' here means without: the following letters are to be taken away from the rest
the letters to be removed come in a strange order, so they need not appear as a block
a surprising outcome is an unexpected one, so what is left is rearranged unexpectedly

blocks.note: taken as written; these four letters are removed in any order

explanation.surface: A critic finds classical English verse unexpectedly and oddly poetic.
explanation.walkthrough: CLASSICAL plus E, with L, E, S, S struck out, leaves CAICAL, which rearranges to ALCAIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcaic verse is a Greek lyric metre named after the poet Alcaeus, so the word describes a particular poetic form.

clue.text: Having a tax that's unbelievable I ab'orred

blocks.note: the apostrophe drops the H of abhorred, so hated loses its H too

explanation.surface: Someone who pays an absurd tax says they hate it, in a dropped-aitch accent.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in ab'orred is the signal: a speaker who drops the H says 'ated for hated.
explanation.definitionFit: Talliated is an old word for subjected to a tallage, a feudal tax, so it means bearing a levy.

clue.text: Chilly precipitation's coming up, bringing nerves

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: sleet is icy rain; the 's is kept as part of the word

explanation.surface: Cold sleet arriving makes everyone tense and edgy.
explanation.definitionFit: To nerve yourself is to steel yourself, both meaning to brace for something difficult.

clue.text: Smart demo contrived to gain absolute control

indicators.note: something contrived is artificially arranged, so the letters are set out anew

explanation.surface: A slick staged protest is a ploy for seizing total power.
explanation.definitionFit: Masterdom is the state of being master, that is supremacy or dominion over others.

clue.text: In the manner of rot burning slowly

blocks.note: as means like or in the way of

explanation.surface: Something decays the way a smouldering fire burns.
explanation.definitionFit: Asmoulder is a predicative adjective meaning smouldering, giving off smoke without flame.

clue.text: Police arrest getting last character carted off

indicators.note: carting off the last character means the final letter is removed

blocks.note: an arrest of movement is a stasis

explanation.surface: An officer makes an arrest and the final suspect is driven away.
explanation.walkthrough: The Stasi was the secret police of East Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stasi was East Germany's state security service, a political police force.

clue.text: Nothing right in the unfilled cake

indicators.note: an unfilled word has its middle emptied, leaving only its outside letters
in places the first pieces inside the following word

blocks.note: nothing is zero, a round letter
Rt is an abbreviation of right

explanation.surface: A cake with no filling is, rightly, nothing much.
explanation.definitionFit: A torte is a rich layered cake, from German.

clue.text: Minister that is getting married is subjected to criticism

blocks.note: id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A clergyman who weds finds himself the subject of critical comment.
explanation.definitionFit: A book or film that has been reviewed has been critically appraised in print.

clue.text: Printer's mark fades — is placed at the bottom

indicators.note: in a down entry, being put at the bottom means coming last in the column

blocks.note: a sound dies away when it fades

explanation.surface: A printer notes that a mark fades and sinks to the foot of the page.
explanation.definitionFit: A diesis is the double dagger, a reference mark used by printers for footnotes.

clue.text: The old lament when soldiers have captured island

indicators.note: a captured thing is held inside its captors

blocks.note: soldiers as the men of the ranks

explanation.surface: An old dirge sung when troops take an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old' marks an archaic word; mein (also mene) is an old Scots and northern word for to lament.
explanation.definitionFit: Mein is an obsolete verb meaning to mourn or bewail, an archaic synonym of lament.

clue.text: Fresh intelligence of the Parisian Match

explanation.surface: Up-to-date news from Paris Match, the French magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Paris Match is a French news weekly, which disguises the split into 'Parisian' and 'Match'.
explanation.definitionFit: The latest is the most recent news, so it is fresh intelligence in the sense of information.

clue.text: Mineral store I'd established, depleted at either end

indicators.note: when the phrase is depleted at both ends, only the stretch in its middle is left to read

blocks.note: the phrase with letters cut away at the front and back

explanation.surface: A dealer says the mineral shop they set up has run low at both ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Oreide is a gold-coloured brass alloy, loosely a mineral substance used in cheap jewellery.

clue.text: Musical character revealing opening, not closing

indicators.note: the closing letter is not included, so the word loses its end

blocks.note: a cleft is a split or opening

explanation.surface: A musical performer shows an overture but never the finale.
explanation.definitionFit: A clef is the symbol at the start of a stave fixing pitch, a character of musical notation.

clue.text: One day in Paris when going round avenue an old coin is found

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it

explanation.surface: On a Paris stroll around an avenue, someone picks up an antique coin.
explanation.walkthrough: MARDI is French for Tuesday; 'One day in Paris' points to a French word, not to a date or an anecdote.
explanation.definitionFit: The maravedi was an old Spanish coin, at last of copper and very little value.

clue.text: "How much does ____?" asks pub customer Herb

blocks.note: surface: a drinker asks the price of something, with a word missing
setter's reading: the gap holds the drink the pub customer is pricing plus the verb for its price

explanation.surface: A pub drinker asks the barman the price of the drink, and the drinker's name is Herb.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap the way a pub customer would: the drink plus the verb for its price, run together.
explanation.definitionFit: Alecost is costmary, an aromatic herb once used to flavour beer, hence its name.

clue.text: Muscle twitching when stuck in bit of furniture at ground level

indicators.note: something stuck in is lodged inside another thing

blocks.clueFragment: bit of furniture at ground level
blocks.note: a caster is a small wheel on a chair or table leg
rapid eye movement, the twitching of sleep

explanation.surface: A muscle starts twitching when you get caught under low furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twitching' looks like an anagram signal, but it stands for REM, the rapid eye movement of sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: The cremaster is the muscle that raises and lowers the testis.

clue.text: A cairn has unusual sort of plant

indicators.note: an unusual version departs from the normal order of things

explanation.surface: A pile of stones on a hillside harbours an odd plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Anacharis is a waterweed, the Canadian pondweed, so it is a kind of plant.

clue.text: Old pram I flogged in advertising exercise?

indicators.note: something flogged is beaten about, knocking its letters out of place

explanation.surface: Someone sold their old pram through an advert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flogged' looks like sold, which fits the advertising surface, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A mail drop is a delivery of leaflets to many letterboxes, a common way to advertise; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Restricts the loins

blocks.note: first meaning: holds back, as a rider checks a horse
second meaning: an old word for the kidneys or lower back

explanation.walkthrough: The biblical sense of the word, for the kidneys and loins, survives in older translations.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for curbing and checking, and an archaic plural noun for the kidneys or loins.

clue.text: Cellist in informal attire not appropriate for top person

indicators.note: the letter used to mark what suits the upper class is left out

explanation.surface: A cellist's informal outfit is unsuitable for a VIP.
explanation.walkthrough: U stands for upper-class, a label for what suits top people; it is removed. Pablo Casals was a famous Catalan cellist.
explanation.definitionFit: Pablo Casals was among the greatest cellists of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Lout was badly taken in, just made miserable once

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so these letters are jumbled
to be taken in is to be held inside something

blocks.note: a ned is a Scottish hooligan

explanation.surface: A lout who was cruelly fooled has been left recently unhappy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' marks an archaic word: new-sad, Spenserian for freshly saddened.
explanation.definitionFit: Newsad is an old compound meaning recently saddened, that is freshly made unhappy.

clue.text: Piano playing harsh in tone with note oddly missing

indicators.note: oddly picks the letters in odd-numbered positions
the chosen letters go missing from the longer word

explanation.surface: A pianist's playing sounds harsh, with one note strangely absent.
explanation.definitionFit: Stride is a jazz piano style with a striding left hand, so it names a manner of piano playing.

clue.text: Certain plants — rodents will eat half of them up

indicators.note: half of a word keeps only one of its two halves, here the back one
in a down entry, up means read from bottom to top
what is eaten ends up inside the eater

blocks.note: the second half of the word

explanation.surface: Rodents will devour half of a certain group of plants.
explanation.definitionFit: A ramet is a single member of a clone of plants, so ramets are particular plants.

clue.text: Function in which you'll see this writer smoke

indicators.note: what can be seen in something lies inside it

blocks.note: the hyperbolic secant, a mathematical function

explanation.surface: A writer says you can see them in a social function, smoking.
explanation.walkthrough: SECH is the hyperbolic secant in mathematics.
explanation.definitionFit: Smeech is a dialect word, from the West Country, for thick smoke or fumes.

clue.text: Time despicable person admitted mistakes

indicators.note: something admitted is let in, so placed inside

blocks.note: an era is a period of time
a rat is a contemptible person

explanation.surface: In time a scoundrel owned up to his errors.
explanation.definitionFit: Errata are printing errors listed for correction, so the word means mistakes.

clue.text: Author, the fellow with hesitation to pen lines

indicators.note: to pen something is to shut it in an enclosure

blocks.note: L for line, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A writer hesitates before putting lines on paper.
explanation.walkthrough: HE and ER together surround LL. Joseph Heller wrote Catch-22.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Heller was the American novelist who wrote Catch-22.

clue.text: Shown to have discarded red outside covering no longer used

indicators.note: what is discarded is thrown away, removed from the word

blocks.note: the letters of red, sitting on the outside of the word

explanation.surface: An unwanted red outer coat is shown being discarded.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove R E from the front and D from the back, the outside of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Veale is an obsolete spelling of veil, a covering for the face.

clue.text: Short slightly crazy tribute

indicators.note: a word cut short loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A brief, rather mad tribute to someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Scatt was a land tax or tribute paid in Orkney and Shetland, from Old Norse.

clue.text: Something poetic from significant orator

indicators.note: the answer is taken from within the following words

explanation.surface: A poetic line from a major public speaker.

clue.text: Set up genuine fortification

explanation.surface: Someone builds a proper defensive wall.

clue.text: One hundred of the stars in camp

explanation.surface: A hundred celebrities are staying in a camp.

clue.text: Rogue president once to rave stutteringly

blocks.note: Abe Lincoln, a former US president
rant with the first letter stuttered

clue.text: Force no longer wrong

a cup tie is a match

explanation.surface: A cautious football side, a player down, heads into a match.

clue.text: What's used by surgeon apt to go wrong with a "Sorry!"
